title: Hedge (Multiplicative Weights): Blending a Handful of Simple Trading Rules Online
text:
Introduction
Every trader who's ever coded more than one rule has hit the same wall: the MA cross catches trends, the RSI reversion catches chop, and neither one works when the market decides to switch character halfway through your backtest window. The usual fix is to pick one and live with its blind spots, or to hardcode some kind of regime filter that's really just another rule guessing at the market's mood.
An older idea from online learning handles this more honestly. Instead of picking a winner up front, you let a small set of simple rules vote every bar, track how each one has actually performed across the whole run, and shift trust toward whichever ones have been right most consistently - without ever needing to know in advance which regime you're in. The algorithm is called Hedge, sometimes written as the multiplicative-weights method. It was introduced by Freund and Schapire in the mid-1990s as a way to combine expert predictions with a worst-case performance guarantee, and it later became one of the building blocks behind AdaBoost. The guarantee that matters here: over any sequence of outcomes, Hedge's cumulative loss can't fall too far behind the single best expert in hindsight, no matter how adversarial the sequence looks - you don't need to know which rule will be right ahead of time, only that the algorithm will find out fast enough not to matter much.
That guarantee is a regret bound on directional accuracy, not a profitability guarantee, and the difference matters. Regret measures how much worse the ensemble's bar-by-bar direction calls were than the best single expert's calls over the full horizon. It does not say whether either approach makes money after spread, stops, position sizing, and confidence thresholds. A system can have provably low regret on direction and still lose money, if every expert it blends loses money while calling direction reasonably well.
What Hedge promises is narrower than it sounds: whatever directional edge exists among your five rules - which one calls the next bar's sign most accurately over the full run, not which is most profitable - the ensemble will find and lean into it almost as well as if you'd known in advance which rule to trust for the entire horizon. That comparator is the single best
fixed
expert over the whole run, not whichever expert is best in the current regime; standard Hedge has no forgetting mechanism, so it carries no formal guarantee of tracking a changing regime, only of eventually catching up to whichever single rule would have been best from the start.
This isn't a full multi-armed-bandit implementation and it isn't a neural net. It's a five-line update rule bolted onto five deliberately dumb trading rules - MA cross, RSI reversion, a Bollinger breakout, a MACD histogram sign, and a Donchian channel breakout - built to show whether adaptive blending earns its keep against the two obvious alternatives: a static equal-weight blend, and trading one of the five rules alone, unblended. All three get tested here, on the same data, with the same risk code underneath them.
I'll walk through the update rule, the code that implements it, and then the part that actually matters: eighteen real Strategy Tester runs across three symbols, two timeframes, and all three blending modes, followed by a full sweep of the one input that theory says should matter most. The results are not a clean "adaptive always wins" story, and I'm reporting them exactly as they came out of the tester.

Why blend instead of picking a winner
Say you've got five simple signals and you don't want to spend your life re-optimizing which one to trust this quarter. You could equal-weight them - average their votes and call it a day - which is robust but dumb: it treats a signal that's been dead wrong for three months exactly the same as one that's been dead right. Or you could pick the single best performer over some lookback window and switch to it, which chases whatever just worked and gets whipsawed the moment the regime turns.
Hedge sits between those two. Every expert's absolute weight shrinks when it's wrong and grows when it's right, and the update is multiplicative rather than additive - a run of wrong calls shrinks a weight exponentially, not linearly, so a consistently bad signal gets starved out fast without ever being deleted. That's accumulated accuracy over the entire run, not a recency-weighted score: a correct call from bar 50 contributes exactly as much to the exponent as one from bar 5,000, and nothing gives the last few bars extra pull beyond whatever accuracy they add to the running total. Worth flagging now too: because weights renormalize to sum to 1 after every update, an expert's
relative
weight can rise on a bar it got wrong, if the other four were more wrong on that same bar - "moves toward accuracy" describes the trend across many bars, not a guarantee on every single one. If the market later proves a demoted signal right again, its weight recovers from wherever it was, no re-initialization required. Nothing here needs to know what "trending" or "ranging" means; it only needs each bar's realized direction.
The exponential part is what separates this from a simple rolling win-rate score. An additive scheme - add a point for a right call, subtract one for a wrong call - treats every mistake the same, regardless of how confident the ensemble currently is in that expert. A multiplicative scheme compounds: an expert already down to a small weight gets punished by a smaller absolute amount for its next mistake (the punishment is a fraction of its current weight, not a fixed increment), while an expert near its starting weight takes a proportionally bigger hit for the same mistake. In practice that means the ensemble demotes a losing rule quickly but doesn't grind an already-marginal rule to zero over one bad patch - there's always a path back if the market turns in its favor again.
The math: multiplicative weights in one paragraph
Each expert
i
casts a vote v_i(t) ∈ {-1, 0, +1} for bar t. Once the bar closes and the real direction is known, every expert gets scored against what actually happened:
l_i(t) =
0.5
-
0.5
· v_i(t) · sign(t)
That's 0 when the vote was right, 1 when it was flat-out wrong, and 0.5 when the expert abstained or the bar was flat. That 0.5 is a design choice worth naming, not a neutral default: an expert that abstains because it genuinely sees no edge is scored as if it had been half wrong, so a rule that abstains often but is never wrong when it does vote can still lose weight relative to one that always votes and is right only slightly more than half the time. This implementation doesn't distinguish "abstains accurately" from "votes mediocrely." The weight update is then:
w_i(t+
1
) = w_i(t) ·
exp
(-η · l_i(t)), renormalized so Σw_i =
1
η is the learning rate, and it's the one knob this whole system lives or dies by - too small and the ensemble barely reacts to anything; too large and it overreacts to single-bar noise and effectively becomes a single-expert system that just changes its mind constantly. Online-learning theory gives a regret bound that names a specific value: η = √(8·ln(N)/T), where N is the number of experts and T is the horizon in bars you're planning to run. With 5 experts and a 2000-bar horizon that comes out to roughly 0.080, and that's what the EA computes automatically when InpEta is left at its default of 0. Section 12 is where I actually test whether that theoretical value holds up against real market data, and the answer is more interesting than "yes."
Notice what T actually does in that formula: it isn't the number of bars in your backtest, it's the horizon you tell the formula to plan for, via the InpRegretHorizon input. A larger horizon lowers eta - the bound gets more conservative the longer a stretch of adversarial outcomes it has to survive - while a smaller horizon raises it, letting the ensemble react faster because it's only promising to keep up over a shorter stretch. That's a real design choice hiding inside a single input: telling the formula you're planning for 2,000 bars produces a meaningfully different eta than telling it 20,000 would, on the exact same five experts.
Five experts, one vote each
Every expert is deliberately simple and returns exactly {-1, 0, +1} - no fractional confidence, no extra state. Simplicity here is the point: if the blend does anything useful, it should be visible as weights shifting between plain, well-understood rules, not hidden inside a smarter single model. Each one covers a different, well-worn idea in technical trading, and none of them is meant to be impressive on its own - the MA cross catches sustained directional moves, RSI reversion catches overextension snapping back, the Bollinger and Donchian breakouts both catch a price pushing outside its recent range but measure that range two different ways, and the MACD histogram catches a shift in short-term momentum before price itself has clearly turned. Overlap between them is expected and even useful: it's what gives the ensemble something real to arbitrate between rather than five independent opinions with nothing in common.

One limitation worth stating plainly rather than letting the name imply more than the code does: HdgDonchian is called with shift=1, and HdgVoteDonchian then tests that same shift-1 close against the channel it just built - so the channel window includes the very bar the vote is cast on. That's closer to "did this bar close at the extreme of its own window" than a textbook breakout, which would test the close against a channel built strictly from the bars
before
it. It's still look-ahead-free - nothing here peeks forward - but it's not quite the classic definition the name suggests. I'm documenting that here rather than quietly changing the shift, because doing so would alter this expert's vote on every bar of every backtest in Section 10, and the published numbers would no longer describe the code shipped here. Decide on purpose which definition you want before trusting the label.

The votes an expert casts this bar can't be scored until next bar's close reveals whether they were right, so they get parked in m_prev_votes and scored one tick later - this is what keeps the whole system look-ahead-free.

EnsembleSignal is where the three test modes actually diverge - MODE_HEDGE uses the learned m_w weights, MODE_EQUAL_WEIGHT overrides every weight to a flat 1/N on the spot without touching m_w itself, and MODE_SINGLE_EXPERT ignores the ensemble entirely and just returns one expert's raw vote. Using the same EA in all three modes on identical data is what makes an apples-to-apples comparison possible later. The indicator handles, risk code, and order-sending path are identical; only the blend-mode dropdown in the Inputs tab changes between one Strategy Tester pass and the next. That's deliberate: any difference in the results has to come from how the votes get combined, not from three different pieces of code doing three different things underneath.
Wiring it into an Expert Advisor
The EA's job is mostly bookkeeping: collect five votes, score last bar's votes before trusting new ones, publish the resulting weights, and trade only when the blended signal clears a confidence threshold.

None of those risk/execution numbers were tuned against this data - they're reasonable round-number defaults (1% risk, a 2x/3x ATR stop/take pair, a 0.20 confidence floor), not swept for a best fit. A sensitivity check on InpConfidence or the ATR multiples could move every number in Section 10 up or down, and no such sweep has been run - the same open gap as the eta sweep in Section 12, just on different inputs. Treat them as worth testing on your own instrument, not as settings this article already validated.

The auto-eta line is the regret bound from Section 4, computed from the expert count and horizon rather than left as a magic number - leaving InpEta at 0 is what makes every run in the matrix use the theoretical value by default. One detail the formula in Section 4 doesn't show: MathMax(InpRegretHorizon,10) floors the horizon at 10 bars, so an unreasonably small InpRegretHorizon can't blow up eta into something absurd. At the 2000-bar default used throughout this article, that floor never engages - it only matters if you set InpRegretHorizon below 10 yourself.

up
to the broker minimum silently takes on more risk than the input asked for. The margin-clamping loop that follows does the same kind of thing at the account level: it checks the real margin requirement OrderCalcMargin returns against actual free margin, and steps the lot size down one volume step at a time until the trade fits or the size drops below the broker's minimum, at which point it gives up rather than sending an order the account can't support. Testing it honestly: an 18-run matrix
One comparator distinction worth nailing down first: Section 4's regret bound is against the single best expert in hindsight, but MODE_SINGLE_EXPERT below runs only the MA-cross expert (InpSingleIdx at its default of 0) - a fixed, naive baseline, not the actual best of the five after the fact. So read "beats the single-expert baseline" below as "beats trading MA-cross alone."
An adaptive-blending claim is exactly the kind of edge claim that falls apart on a single symbol and timeframe, so this got tested across all three blend modes ( MODE_HEDGE, MODE_EQUAL_WEIGHT, MODE_SINGLE_EXPERT - the last with the MA-cross expert as the naive baseline) on three symbols (EURUSD, GBPUSD, XAUUSD) and two timeframes (H1, M15) - eighteen single-pass Strategy Tester runs total, every one at the EA's shipped default inputs, over the identical 2026.01.01-2026.09.01 window, every-tick modeling against real ticks, a $10,000 deposit at 1:100 leverage. Nothing here is optimized to look good; the eighteen numbers are what the tester actually returned.
Reproducing those numbers needs the full testing environment spelled out, not just the inputs - here it is, without naming the broker:

EURUSD and GBPUSD check whether a pattern is a genuine property of the approach or just one pair's quirk - though they aren't statistically independent, both USD pairs that tend to move together, so a pattern on both is one pattern seen twice, not two confirmations. XAUUSD adds a different price scale and volatility profile, which mattered more than blend mode once the results came in. H1 and M15 share the identical InpRegretHorizon of 2000 bars, and the calendar coverage matters: FX/CFD trades roughly 24 hours a day, five days a week, about 120 H1 bars and 480 M15 bars per week.
That puts 2000 H1 bars at under four months, 2000 M15 bars at just over four weeks - roughly four times more calendar time on H1 than M15, the mismatch Section 12 investigates. Summed across all eighteen runs, the matrix produced 8,599 total trades, past the few-hundred-trade floor worth seeing before any backtest is worth reading - but those trades are pooled across three symbols, two timeframes and three modes, so the total doesn't establish reliability for any single comparison; each cell still stands on its own, smaller count.

None of the six combinations produced a net profit for any of the three modes - this isn't a system to trade as shipped, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. The more useful question was never "does Hedge make money," it was "does adapting the blend beat the two obvious static alternatives," and the honest answer is: sometimes, in a pattern worth taking seriously rather than dismissing as noise - with a caveat attached that I'd rather state than skip.
On both FX pairs, the result flips cleanly by timeframe: Hedge loses to equal-weight on H1 (EURUSD and GBPUSD both), but beats it clearly on M15 (same two pairs, same direction, same margin) - one pattern seen twice on correlated pairs, worth taking seriously, not an independently replicated result. The likely reason is that the H1 and M15 auto-eta are both computed from the same 2000-bar regret horizon, which (Section 10) covers roughly four times more calendar time on H1 than on M15 - so the same theoretical rate ends up better matched to how fast the M15 regime actually shifts, a theory Section 12's sweep goes on to test directly. A genuinely independent check - an uncorrelated pair, or enough symbols for a real significance test - is the obvious next step before leaning on this harder than "repeated twice on related pairs" supports.
The single-expert baseline isn't a strawman that reliably loses either - it beat Hedge outright on GBPUSD H1, and on XAUUSD H1 it posted the lowest net loss and drawdown of the three despite the lowest profit factor
